title: Services & Dependency Injection: Handed Dependencies, Not Constructed Ones
oneLiner: A class that builds its own dependencies is stuck with them forever; a class that receives its dependencies through its constructor (the special method that runs when an object is created with new) can be handed a completely different one without changing a single line.
keyTakeaway: Dependency injection isn't really about a fancy DI container or framework -- it's the simple idea that a class should RECEIVE the things it depends on (usually through its constructor) instead of constructing them itself, which is what makes swapping a real implementation for a fake/test one possible without touching the class's own code at all.
explanation:
A "service" in modern app architecture is usually a small, focused class that does ONE job (send an email, read from a database, call an external API, the set of operations another system lets your code call) and holds little or no state of its own between calls. The naive way to USE a service inside another class is to construct it directly, right where it's needed -- `var emailer = new SmtpEmailService(); emailer.Send(...)`. That works, but it permanently welds this class to SmtpEmailService specifically: there's no way to test this class without ALSO sending a real email, and no way to swap in a different email provider without editing this class's source code.

DEPENDENCY INJECTION flips that: instead of constructing its own dependency, a class RECEIVES it -- usually through its constructor -- as anything satisfying an interface (see Interfaces & Abstraction). The class doing the receiving never constructs an SmtpEmailService or a FakeEmailService directly; it just calls `.Send()` (or `.Notify()`) on whatever it was handed. That single change is what makes it possible to hand a real service in production and a fake, no-op service in a test, with the exact same class code running unmodified either way.

ASP.NET Core apps do exactly this in Program.cs: `builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>(...)` registers the database context as a service, and every endpoint that needs it just asks for an AppDbContext parameter. ASP.NET Core's built-in DI container constructs it and hands it over, and the endpoint code never calls `new AppDbContext()` itself.
